title: Origin Ambiguity
text:
Differences between Human and AI origin
Ability to differentiate between human origin and AI origin
Consequences of ambiguity of origin
Legal grounds for disclosure



The difference in pereption of materials with human origin compared to materials with AI origin has been researched on several domains:

Trustworthiness: generally speaking, people trust humans more than AI
Purchase Intentions: Generally, people are less willing to purchase a product, are less loyal to a product, and are less willing to recommend a product, if they know that AI has been used in connotation with this product in any way
Attribution & Responsibility: People think AI is more mechanistic, and therefore attribute less bias and more analytical. They also adapt their behavior in response to it.







TipTrustworthiness






people trust AI less than humans in various contexts:

AI is perceived to lack human abilities (Kirk and Givi 2025; Lefkeli, Karataş, and Gürhan-Canli 2024)

which leads to perceived human decision-makers in the background, which in turn leads to perceived reduction in privacy and increase in feeling exploitet (Lefkeli, Karataş, and Gürhan-Canli 2024)

AI is perceived as less private (Lefkeli, Karataş, and Gürhan-Canli 2024)
trust is decreased more if AI use is disclosed (Schilke and Reimann 2025; Kirk and Givi 2025) …
… and people trust AI less when disclosing things (Lefkeli, Karataş, and Gürhan-Canli 2024)

some of these effects (e.g. algorithm aversion (Bigman 2022)) have been discussed extensively already
Pfeuffer et al. (2025) show that disclosing the alteration of images decreases trust in content creators / brands







NoteNote Jonas



This is basically “done” at least from the POV of getting any of this published. Trust as an attitude is a pretty basic and thus relatively uninteresting variable imo. It is just a positively valenced variable that can capture both cognitive and affective dimensions, thus it might work as mediator whenever there is either a positive or negative outcome.











TipPurchase Intention






the use of AI decreases the intention to purchase a product, the product loyalty and the willingness to recommend a product

if communication is perceived to be written by AI (Kirk and Givi 2025)
if generated imagery is generated by AI (Belanche et al. 2025)

especially for hedonic services (Belanche et al. 2025)

… but if people trust AI, the effect is mitigated (Jung et al. 2025)
… and perceived humanness of AI increases purchase intention (Jung et al. 2025)








NoteNote Jonas



My general suggestion would be to look at something that goes beyond purchase/acceptance. The dominant paradigm over the last years has been this aversion vs. acceptance debate. I think we have considerably more upside, if we focus on a more up- or downstream variable along consumers’ journeys with AI (which can be a variable with impact on business or consumers’ self concept etc.). That means, we think about something that is prior to acceptance or not directly relevant to it or we look at usage/interaction etc.











TipAttribution, Responsibility & Behavior








because AI is perceived as lacking human abilities (Lefkeli, Karataş, and Gürhan-Canli 2024; Bigman 2022), responsibility is shifted to “humans in the background”
This leads to perceiving AI as less biased …(Feldkamp et al. 2024; Bigman 2022; Bonezzi and Ostinelli 2021; Bedemariam and Wessel 2023)
… and to less moral outcry when AI makes “biased” decisions (Feldkamp et al. 2024; Bigman 2022; Bonezzi and Ostinelli 2021; Bedemariam and Wessel 2023)





People display themselves as more analytical when they believe they are assessed by AI instead of humans (Goergen, De Bellis, and Klesse 2025)
… (more phenomena in that direction to be researched)





As all of these dimensions have become rather saturated in research over the last couple of years, we will not be focusing our own research on these domains, but use them as a foundation of research already demonstrating various aspects that are different when it comes to Humans vs. AI.



Humans are generally not good at differenciating between AI and human origin. This research goes back several years. As much of the AI generated materials only gets better and less distinguishable from human origin, it is to be assumed that these effects will become even more pronounced in the future.






TipPrimary Sources on Ability to Differenciate






“almost 50% of respondents can distinguish between AI and human generated artwork.” (Vukojičić, Krstić, and Veinović 2023)
“participants performed below chance levels in identifying AI-generated poems (46.6% accuracy)” (Porter and Machery 2024) “participants were more likely to judge AI-generated poems as human-authored than actual human-authored poems (Porter and Machery 2024)
non-artists have pronounced difficulty identifying AI generated images (Ha et al. 2024), but artists and professional artists had much less difficulty (Ha et al. 2024)
However, You et al. (2024) did not find a difference between creators and non-creators in accuracy of identifying images
AI generated image detectors (e.g. Hive) had no difficulty detecting AI generated images (Ha et al. 2024)
With training, participants were able to correctly identify AI generated text correctyl 65% of the time; without training 55% - i.e. slightly above chance (Milička et al. 2025)







Legally, there are few laws regulating the mandated disclosure of AI when generating materials. While there are laws, regulations and acts in relation to the use of AI, they are not necessarily applicable to marketing material for several reasons (Vischer, 2024).
When it comes to assessment or data manipulation using AI, there are strict provisions – at least in the EU (GDPR), Switzerland (FADP), and some other nations (e.g. UK, Australia). While they were not written with the use of AI tools as their primary scope, they apply as soon as personal data is obtained from a consumer, and mandate the disclosure of the use and purpose of this data, as well as any third parties this data is shared with (such as OpenAI when using ChatGPT.)
Many companies increasingly utilize AI when generating marketing and informational materials due to its cost- and time efficiency. At the same time, research indicates that consumers generally trust companies less when the use of AI is disclosed. Therefore, it is to be assumed that there is an incentive to not diclose the use of AI on the companies side.






TipRegulations pertaining to Personal Data






GDPR / FADP as part of the duty to inform people when personal data is obtained to be used with any sort of AI system (GDPR Art. 13/14, FADP Art. 19ff)
and for which purposes (GDPR Art. 5(1) and FADP Art. 6(2-3))
as well as in the context of consent (GDPR Art. 4(11) & FADP Art. 6(6))










TipRegulations pertaining to Competition






Swiss Labour Act (Ordinance 3, Art. 26) prohibits behavioral monitoring in the workplace unless required. In that case they must be disclosed (Ordinance 3, Art. 6)
Federal Act on Cartels and other Restraints of Competition and the Federal Act on Unfair Competition(CH) provides some regulations on transparency, copyright of competitors, and targeting (CartA,UCA)










TipThe EU AI Act





Providers shall ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed in such a way that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, taking into account the circumstances and the context of use. This obligation shall not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties, unless those systems are available for the public to report a criminal offence.
Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content, shall ensure that the outputs of the AI system are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.
Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake, shall disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. This obligation shall not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offence.
Where the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme, the transparency obligations set out in this paragraph are limited to disclosure of the existence of such generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work.
The information referred to in paragraphs 1 to 4 shall be provided to the natural persons concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure.
AI Act, Art. 50









TipAdditional Laws specifically pertaining to AI






The United States have several state-wide bills which regulate some uses of AI (e.g. AI transparency Act in California or the Colorado AI Act).








People prefer human over AI
Organizations and Companies tend to prefer AI over human due to efficiency and cost*
People are bad at identifying AI generated content
The law does not provide clear regulations on the (mandated) disclosure of AI, and research shows that AI disclosure decreases trust and purchase intention \(\rightarrow\) motivation for companies to not disclose the use of AI

*although it must be noted that many of these AI applications are still works in progress as well, and this sentiment could very well shift
Therefore, we should assume that companies try to incorporate AI without disclosing it to keep their reputation, whereas consumers prefer human-origin content. Giving companies the benefit of the doubt, we should assume that this conflict happens in situations where law does not prescribe unambiguous behavior (i.e. in information, marketing and branding; but not in assessment or evaluation).

title: Origin Ambiguity
text:
Definitions

Def. Ambiguity: “Ambiguity is the type of meaning in which a phrase, statement, or resolution is not explicitly defined, making for several interpretations; others describe it as a concept or statement that has no real reference. A common aspect of ambiguity is uncertainty. It is thus an attribute of any idea or statement whose intended meaning cannot be definitively resolved, according to a rule or process with a finite number of steps.” Wikipedia


Def. Origin Ambiguity: Origin ambiguity occurrs when the origin of something generated (text, speech, video, image, or otherwise) cannot be definively resolved*. (current working definition, definitely subject to change!)

*The term origin ambiguity was chosen purposefully over authorship ambiguity, as current law in copyright does not intend for any AI tool to be able to author and therefore own content.

title: Origin Ambiguity
text:
Ambiguity Aversion
People are generally averse to ambiguity. However, while these effects replicate outside of the lab to some extent, they are not as clear-cut as one would think, especially in situations where the risky situation has low winning probabilities or the situaiton pertains to losses. Furthermore, studies on external validity of the effect reveal mixed results.






TipPrimary Sources on Ambiguity Aversion






introduced with the Ellsberg paradox in 1961
in principle, people prefer the less ambiguous (read: uncertain) bet when provided with several options despite the choice being irrational (Machina and Siniscalchi 2014)
The concept of “ambiguity aversion” is not unanimously defined (Machina and Siniscalchi 2014), however in “traditional literature”, it most often means a preference for known risks over unknown risks(Trautmann and Van De Kuilen 2015)

ambiguity aversion is not universal: when introducing losses or lower likelihoods, ambiguity aversion is neutralized or even sought after (Kocher, Lahno, and Trautmann 2018) \(\rightarrow\) see also: Kocher (2014), Binmore, stewart & Voorhoeve (2012), Kahn & Sarin (1997)
much of this literature has focused on gain-frames (i.e. winning something)
however, when the risky urn is a high risk urn, people seem to prefer the ambiguous urn (Curly & Yates, cited in Trautmann and Van De Kuilen (2015))
“A significant number of studies found a complete reversal of ambiguity attitudes between the (modest‐likelihood) gain and loss domain, with ambiguity seeking for losses (Abdellaoui, Vossmann, & Weber, 2005; Baillon & Bleichrodt, 2012; Casey & Scholz, 1991; Chakravarty & Roy, 2009; Ho, Keller, & Keltyca, 2002; Kothiyal, Spinu, & Wakker, 2012).” (Trautmann and Van De Kuilen, 2015, p. 105) (pdf)

there are also studies on natural ambiguity (e.g. an American prefers to bet on the Dow Jones index, Trautmann and Van De Kuilen (2015))

In many of these events, it is shown that people feel more knowledgeable about the event(s) they are familiar with, and also assign higher subjective probabilities to them

ambiguity aversion is contested to be a higher-order effect in itself \(\rightarrow\) ambiguity prudence and ambiguity temperance suggested as higher order effects (Baillon, Schlesinger, and Van De Kuilen 2018)
ambiguity aversion is also subclassified into absolute and relative ambiguity aversion (Baillon and Placido 2019)
many potential moderators are suggested for ambiguity attitudes:

comparative ignorance
peer effects
group decisions
market interaction
many more (Trautmann and Van De Kuilen 2015)

title: Origin Ambiguity
text:
Ambiguity in Marketing
Ambiguity is a topic that has been discussed in the marketing context extensively and from different lenses. Ambiguity aversion (for general details see above) has shown to correlate to preference for established products (Muthukrishnan, Wathieu, and Xu 2009), and as a moderator to consumer satisfaction [Yi (1993);Erdem and Keane (1996); and others]. Ambiguity is also discussed as a purposeful marketing tactic (Kovacheva and Nikolova 2024).






TipAmbiguity Aversion and Preference for Established Products






ambiguity aversion correlates with preference for more established / well known brands (Muthukrishnan, Wathieu, and Xu 2009)
induced ambiguity aversion also predicts preference for established products later on (Muthukrishnan, Wathieu, and Xu 2009)
established brands sell stronger in situations where information is presented more ambiguously (Muthukrishnan, Wathieu, and Xu 2009)










TipAmbiguity as a Moderator of Consumer Satisfaction






ambiguity in product quality (Yi 1993; Erdem and Keane 1996):

product satisfaction = comparing expectations vs. reality \(\rightarrow\) confirmation / disconfirmation paradigm (Yi 1993)
ambiguous product experience when the quality of the product is difficult to evaluate (Yi 1993)
consumers evaluate products based on a top-down (expectation and theorizing-driven) approach, when the quality is difficult to evaluate (i.e. ambiguous), but follow a data-driven bottom-up approach when the quality is unambiguous (and neglect expectations) (Yi 1993)
ambiguity about product quality is countered by Bayesian learning through the customer (buying different products and updating quality beliefs about \(t-n\) products). Structural modelling of this relationship is better than the Guadagni-Little model, especially the dynamic component appears valuable (Erdem and Keane 1996)
when product quality is ambiguous, consumers rely more on advertising to inform themselves (Hoch and Ha 1986)

this effect is stronger when the ad is shown before showing the product compared to after, implying that there may be some sort of selective retreival of preceding information (Hoch and Ha 1986)


ambiguous marketing offers: ambiguous marketing offers are more effective under scarcity (Dhar et al., 1999), both resource scarcity and availability scarcity (Dhar et al., 1999; Fan et al., 2019)
it also depends on how information is displayed: numeric cognition influences how ambiguity aversion manifests (Lenkovskaya and Sweldens 2025) (compression effect & left digit effect)










TipRole Ambiguity






Def. Role Ambiguity: occurs when a person feels that he or she lacks salient information needed to effectively enact his or her role Singh (1993), p. 12)


highly discussed construct in marketing & management [Singh (1993); Ho et al. (1997); and others]

\(\rightarrow\) not highly relevant to our project









TipAmbiguous (uncertain) Marketing Tactics






surprise boxes, buy and reveal deals, random price promotion, teaser ads
some classification frameworks, e.g. Kovacheva and Nikolova (2024):

assortments: e.g. “loot boxes”
promotional: e.g. “incomplete ads”
innovation: e.g. “mystery flavor coke”

uncertainty marketing is used to cue consumers’ attention and interest (Kovacheva and Nikolova 2024)
important for uncertainty marketing: the concealed information is non-negative, i.e. supposed to piqué someone’s interest, not worry them about the “catch”
the success of uncertainty marketing depends on many intra-personal characteristics

stake: low vs. high
opacity: low vs. high \(\rightarrow\) stakes and opacity seem to be independent (Kovacheva and Nikolova 2024)
the concept of “lower stakes” is also discussed in other literature: Arrow (1965) for monetary stakes, Duke et al. (2018) in conjunction with uncertainty (uncertainty is less tolerable in high-stakes situations)







NoteNote Sabou



While this is not necessarily what we are after, I think the insights regarding stakes could be interesting independent variables for us, i.e. does it matter how high-stakes something is for people to behave differently?

title: Origin Ambiguity
text:
“Origin Ambiguity”
While ambiguity in general has been discussed in various aspects (see sections above), origin ambiguity in terms of not knowing the source of a piece of information has hardly been discussed. There are somewhat related streams of research when looking at what purposefully obfuscating parts of informational material in advertising; when looking at deepfakes (although there is very little research on how people act when they believe something is a deepfake, only how they act when they know it), and (probably most relevant) the uncanny valley effect.






Tip(Origin) Ambiguity due to obfuscated Materials






Studies analyzing how cropped photos, etc. ellicit ambiguity
Peracchio and Meyers-Levy (1994): visual ambiguity is caused by cropped photos

when viewers lack sufficient motivation to parse cropped object, the product evaluations are based on some easily available heuristic (e.g. what the brand claims: “high quality jeans!”) (Peracchio and Meyers-Levy 1994)

Johar (1995) finds similar effects for how the information of an ad is perceived under low- vs. high involvement

it doesn’t matter if the important object itself is cropped, or if something else is cropped, the “cropping effect” (i.e. the ambiguity) is what makes people involved in processing given enough motivation (Peracchio and Meyers-Levy 1994)

Hagtvedt (2011) finds that incomplete typefaces (where letters are obfuscated or left out) ellicit lower trustworthiness, but higher perceived innovativeness

trustworthiness is related to clarity, whereas innovativeness is related to interestingness (\(\rightarrow\) this could be something to explore for AI ads, although this effect here relates to letters of logos!)

Sevilla and Meyer (2020) find that concealing aspects of an aesthetic product in particular can heighten curiosity and ellicit positive associations










TipDeepfakes






deepfakes are generally hard to detect for humans (see primarily Diel et al. (2024) for a meta-analysis showing that humans are practically as good as chance)
there is very little research on the consequences of ambiguity introduced through deepfakes, however:

Köbis, Doležalová, and Soraperra (2021) find that people think a video is genuine rather than a Deepfake more often, and they are overconfident in their decisions
Whittaker et al. (2025) show that perception of AI alteration (with deepfakes) decreases intention to purchase, and humanness of deepfake increases perceived authenticity (there is however no ambiguity in this study, as people knew what they were looking at)
Ahmed, Ng, and Bee (2023) look at the reasons why people share deepfake videos and identify FOMO, low cognitive ability, thinking that they are accurate (duh…)
a different study (Soto-Sanfiel, Angulo-Brunet, and Saha 2024) show that most people who do share deepfakes don’t do so for informational purposes, but for hedonic and entertainment











TipThe uncanny valley Effect






The uncanny valley hypothesis predicts a negative emotional appraisal of human replicas that appear or behave not quite human



the uncanny valley effect is perceived as highly unpleasant (Seyama and Nagayama 2007)
systematic literature reviews and meta-analyses show moderate support in favor of the following relevant effects:

eeriness in movement causes more distress than eeriness in still images (ka?, $?tsyriReviewEmpiricalEvidence2015)
“categorization ambiguity” causes more distress (ka?, $?tsyriReviewEmpiricalEvidence2015)
other studies summarize the ambiguity as “categorical uncertainty hypothesis” (Rau 2020). While there is substantial support in favor of these hypotheses, the uncanny valley effect and its causal mechanisms is still somewhat contested (see for example: (MacDorman and Chattopadhyay 2016))

there are attempts to quantify the predecessants and consequences of the uncanny valley effect, e.g. with a Bayesian framework (Moore 2012)
when we are confronted with the eeriness of the uncanny valley, the amount of information processed is suppressed (Shin, Kim, and Biocca 2019); however this study looks more at the evaluation of the avatars, so maybe not 100% relevant to AI videos










TipOther Related Work





While there is very little (maybe even no?) research on origin ambiguity in marketing, there are a few constructs somewhat relating to it, namely:

authenticity: Silver, Newman, and Small (2021) show that perceived inauthenticity increases outrage at brands. One core driver of perceived inauthenticity is deception, another one is adulteration (i.e. “enhancing”)
obfuscation of information: only providing partial information on a product can go both ways. Research shows that products profiting most are those that have the least to hide (see box on obfuscation above)










NoteNote Jonas



This is interesting. What does feeling ambiguity related to content origin (or something else in AI realm) do with the consumer? Feeling unease, compensatory behavior (in other domain), outrage, what inferences do consumers draw under ambiguity?, how do consumers deal with ambiguity in general –> we probably fall back on some heuristics, can we identify a new one here and any consequences?








NoteIdea Jonas



How many people are actually experiencing this kind of ambiguity? Under TikTok videos (define domain), we could probably find references to “Is this AI?” that would be perfect ambiguity markers. That is descriptive in a first step. But then what other variables could be interesting to look at here? What does this ambiguity do to the video’s performance in terms of engagment etc. (issue will be control group, so potentially just correlative). What are ambiguity markers that consumers mention, what makes them certain of the origin?
Where is the marketing relevance? We either do a pure consumer story (it does something with the consumer, wellbeing, self-concept etc.) or we extrapolate to companies that use AI for ads or so: What does ambiguity do with brand attitudes etc. (there is a gap here, I suppose)

title: Origin Ambiguity
text:
Possible Research Streams (not mutually exclusive)

Stream 1: What causes the origin to be perceived as ambiguous?

We could analyze Reddit data (r/RealorAI, r/isThisAI, …) (\(\rightarrow\) https://www.reddit.com/r/reddit.com/wiki/api/)
We could see if there is a similar way to analyze data from TikTok or Instagram (Instagram Graph API for creator and business accounts could be interesting, because these creators essentially use instagram to market themselves \(\rightarrow\) https://transparency.meta.com/researchtools/meta-content-library; There also seems to be something for TikTok, but I am not familiar with that platform at all: https://developers.tiktok.com/products/research-api/)



Stream 2: How do the behaviors of people change if people are no longer sure?

Are people more attentive (parallels to uncanney valley effects)?

do they watch a video longer?
do they pay more attention (e.g. operationalize through what they remember about video?)

Are people more hesitant/willing to accept information under high/low origin ambiguity?
Do preconceptions and attitudes towards a company or product change how ambiguity is perceived?

hedonic vs. utilitarian products
informative vs. noninformative ads / content

How do people re-calibrate their perspective on information when they are unsure about the origin?







NoteNote Sabou



Discussion with a friend with a background in communication sciences came up with the interesting phenomenon that people on TikTok justify the “validity” of a video with “no, it is real, the information comes from a credible source” wherein traditional (print) media regains a status of validity and authority that has been reduced over the last few years. Not sure if we can or want to spin this thought furhter, but I think it could be an interesting angle.




Stream 3: Are ambiguity effects independent of source (written, spoken, image, video)?

self-explanatory

title: Origin Ambiguity
text:
Dependent Variables / Outcomes

Focus on Company

willingness to purchase product
willingness to pay (does price sensitivity change)
image of company (trustworthiness, …) \(\rightarrow\) could borrow some ideas from social sciences with prosocial perception of companies and counterfactuals



Focus on Consumer

What do people believe?
Do people update their perception / expectation / “reality”?
Perception of content in particular (see note as well)
Why do people care about the origin of a source?
Does the “uncanny valley effect” exist for AI generated videos, and what does it do depending on the context (more aversion, less information processing or more, …?)

title: Origin Ambiguity
section: Possible Moderators and Mediators to consider
text:
Possible Moderators and Mediators to consider

technology knowledge & preconceptions \(\rightarrow\) many studies already control for “technological ability” (esp. when it comes to AI perception)
age \(\rightarrow\) can we expect people of different generations to be perceptive to different aspects of ambiguity (“boomers on facebook” phenomenon)
motivation (tied into the research by Capiocco and colleagues on the use of heuristics in low- vs. high motivation, especially in image materials (Petty, Cacioppo, and Schumann 1983))
further moderators?







NoteNote Jonas



AI specific dependent Variables

We should check if we find something that is specific to AI (artifically in general) generated content as the DV.
One approach would be the probabilistic nature: do we actually ever know? Do people think about that and how does this change?

title: Origin Ambiguity
text:
Possible “Big Questions” to ask

Platform Effects
This would go less for or against a particular company, but platforms which are used by consumers to make purchase decisions. Here, we could explore how people treat ambiguity depending on platform rather than depending on product or brand. It would be a nice playing ground for comparing e.g. various modalities of origin ambiguity (written, image, video). It would also be interesting to see what effects the perception of the platform itself has (e.g. TikTok could be perceived as more entertainment and there is no expectation of informativeness, whereas a tech review blog is expected to be informative).


Perceived Autonomy and Empowerment
This is my attempt at getting away from the “classics” of purchasing behavior, WTS, etc. It could be interesting how consumers perceive themselves when confronted with ambiguity? Do they feel “cheated” on, do they feel disempowered / taken advantage of, or do they not care at all?


Information Processing
This would tie into research on Deepfakes as well as Uncanny Valley Effects. We could have a look at how people process information depending on perceived ambiguity, and also if they engage with info more or less (e.g. do they click on “more info” or whatever, or do they do the opposite and click away / disregard as soon as they are not sure if it is AI or human anymore?)

Summary
The privacy-convenience paradox has been observed and discussed for a long time, but to this day the psychological mechanisms have not been underpinned conclusively. One aspect that would be very interesting would be comparing computational models of various mechanism specifications based on experimental data (and potentially also branching out to correlative designs with real data). Another interesting aspect is the privacy-paradox specifically in terms of AI. There, I see several domains of application: What type of info is shared with ChatBots, how different knowledge and experiences influence this, how privacy and convenience interrelates with agentic AI (this would also go in the same direction as your project with Melandie Clegg which by the way is super interesting as well).

title: Origin Ambiguity
text: As firms increasingly use generative AI to produce product shoots, video ads, and news-like reels, AI-generated outputs reach near-human quality, making it difficult for viewers to distinguish whether content was created by humans or AI. We take a new perspective on this phenomenon and propose origin ambiguity as a central challenge in such contemporary marketing communication. In the absence of clear regulations, consumers increasingly experience ambiguity related to content origin and pose the question “is this AI or real?”. We ask: what changes when people no longer know if what they are looking at has been generated by a human or by AI? To the best of our knowledge, this question remains unanswered. Existing work suggests that ambiguity is a relevant phenomenon with potentially detrimental effects. Specifically, ambiguity might shift attention away from content deliberation toward deliberation about origin, if consumers are motivated enough to engage in deeper processing (e.g., under high involvement), with implications for marketing persuasiveness, informed decision-making, and affective responses (amongst others).

title: Origin Ambiguity
text:
AI and Human Origin
Much research has studied the consequences of explicit human vs. AI origin under the phenomena of algorithm aversion and appreciation (e.g., Bigman (2022)). Here, consumers know and/or are informed about the origin of a recommendation, post, or product, and seem to prefer human over AI or vice versa conditional on various factors. Other research demonstrates that people are generally bad at identifying the origin of content (AI or human) (e.g., Vukojičić, Krstić, and Veinović (2023); Porter and Machery (2024); Milička et al. (2025)).
This latter research points at a human-AI generation frontier that is increasingly blurred. As a case in point, multiple forums exist around the question “Is this AI or real/human” (r/RealOrAI), and the comment sections on social media pages are filled with consumers eager to know if what they are looking at is “real” or AI-generated. Importantly, there is no legally mandated disclosure of AI involvement in content generation, resulting in many situations where the origin remains ambiguous.

title: Origin Ambiguity
text:
Ambiguity in Marketing
Ambiguity in marketing (e.g. surprise boxes) has been shown to affect attention and raise interest, but also result in aversion, especially in high-stakes situations (Kovacheva and Nikolova 2024). For example, when product quality is ambiguous, consumers rely more on ads (Hoch and Ha 1986), and on top-down approaches (i.e. expectations, theories, Yi (1993)); and ambiguity aversion correlates with a preference for established products (Muthukrishnan, Wathieu, and Xu 2009; Hoch and Ha 1986). Furthermore, research on a distinct, but related phenomenon – the uncanny valley (Mori, MacDorman, and Kageki 2012) – gives preliminary evidence that ambiguous stimuli tax cognitive resources (Shin, Kim, and Biocca 2019; Tao et al. 2022; Howard 2017).
One important moderator for the occurrence of ambiguity effects in general are the stakes of a situation and the resulting motivation of consumers to resolve ambiguity. Marketing tactics strategically using obfuscated materials (i.e. cropping objects, incomplete typefaces, …) show that consumers attempt to resolve these introduced ambiguities only when they are motivated to do so Hagtvedt (2011). We expect that comparable effects occur under origin ambiguity.

title: Origin Ambiguity
text:
Theoretical
This phenomenon integrates several streams of research that to the best of our knowledge have been treated separately so far: research on ambiguity in marketing, on cognitive load theory, and on consumer exposure and reactions to AI-generated content. Extending prior work on AI where origin is known or the variable in question, we study cases where humans face content that is neither declared AI or human or easily determined as one or the other.

title: Origin Ambiguity
text:
Practical
Origin ambiguity holds implications for both marketers and consumers: For marketers, potential backfiring of AI generated ads as well as the resulting trade-offs with efficiency and effectiveness are relevant. For consumers, cognitive resource reallocation might come at the cost of informed decision-making.

title: Analysis ESF-Survey
text:
Open Associations

When you browsed through your social media feed, which content-related thoughts crossed your mind?
\(n = 68\) answered this question.

Summary
When we just ask about content-related thoughts, there is little to no associations with origin, origin ambiguity or AI in particular.









Social media content can be created in different ways. When browsing your social media feed, did you wonder how some of the content was created?
\(n = 68\) answered this question.

Summary
When asking specifically about creation of content, we do get some associations with AI:

“AI generated Memes, Edits, Animated videos, Picture-Slideshows”
“at some point yes, because some videos are most likely created with artificial intelligence. But nowadays sometimes you can‘t tell if the content is real or made up.”
” Sometimes there are AI created content, thats more interesting but this time that wasn‘t the case”
and others










How much of the content you consumed in the last few minutes do you remember?









In general, participants reported to not recall much of the content they had just consumed (just under 50%: \(mean_\text{Recall} = 45.877\), (\(SD_\text{Recall} = 27.112\)).
There is a peak around 25%, and a second, smaller peak at 75%.
Recall did not significantly differ between platforms (TikTok, Instagram, Other).










    Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test

data:  recall_selfreport_1 by platform
Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 0.81301, df = 2, p-value = 0.666




Origin Ambiguity
We asked a total of 6 questions pertaining to origin ambiguity:









Most responses were neither skewed in one or the other direction, implying moderate agreement. Surprisingly, our results show a tendency to rather not have experienced origin ambiguity in the past couple of minutes, as indicated by a mean of \(mean_\text{real} = 2.338\) (\(SD_\text{real} = 1.428\)).

title: Analysis ESF-Survey
text:
General Perception
The subsequent questions were asked about participants’ social media feed overall, not the past two minutes.

Thinking about your social media feed overall, what proportion of the content you see is …
















It appears that people think a majority of the content they consume has been created by a human. However, when asked about the involvement of AI, much of the content is perceived as at least augmented by AI. This dichotomy could be resolved in several ways. One possiblity is that participants misunderstood the first question and interpreted “definitely made by AI” as meaning 100% bot accounts without any human involvement. The second possibility is that participants perceive content based on a human-written prompt or base image (augmentation) as still clearly made by a human, although the human had help from AI.


When I am not sure about the origin of the content, I …























While people generally seem to experience origin ambiguity infrequently (as indicated by the questions above), when they experience it, their behavior follows some of the core patterns we hypothesized: People pay more attention to context clues, slightly less attention to the content itself, and go to the comments to inform themselves.

title: Analysis ESF-Survey
text:
Specific Questions
The following questions were asked about participants’ perception of their social media feed they scrolled through just now.

Thinking about your social media feed you scrolled through in the last few minutes, what proportion of the content you saw was …
















When asking participants about the content they just watched, the patterns regarding origin assumptions and augmentation remain the same.


Specific Instances
Of all respondents, \(n = 15\) reported that they recalled a specific instance of content they wondered was generated by AI. \(n = 48\) did report that there was no content generated by AI. In total, \(n = 22\) instances were reported, meaning that some participants recalled more than one instance. The following charts summarize responses across all instances, meaning that certain participants repeat.


Description of the Instance(s)








Reasons Given








Modality and Type
Looking at the modality of content, the overwhelming majority of examples given seems to be videos. Almost all examples stem from the entertainment domain.











Certainty and Involvement
On average, participants were \(mean_\text{certainty} = 61.474, SD_\text{certainty} = 24.939\) certain that the content they were referring to was AI-generated. Additionally, participants tended to say AI was rather more involved than less (\(mean_\text{involvement} = 68.053, SD_\text{certainty} = 31.722\)). The correlation between certainty and involvement is \(r = 0.579964\). However, as visualized in the plot, the number of data points is low and the dispersion is large.

























Reactions
After seeing the content, I …









Reactions to the content again demonstrate that at least some effects we hypothesize seem to occurr: Paying attention to context cues, and looking for additional information.

import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
import pandas as pd


base_url = "https://www.psychologie.uzh.ch"
overview_url = base_url + "/de/bereiche/uebersicht.html"

response = requests.get(overview_url)
soup = BeautifulSoup(response.text,"html.parser")



## Level 1 subpages
subpage_links = []
all_data = []


for link in soup.find_all("a",href=True):
    href = link["href"]
    if href.startswith("/de/bereiche/") and href.endswith(".html"):
        subpage_links.append(base_url+href)
        print(base_url+href)

for subpage_url in subpage_links:
    
    print(f"\nScraping {subpage_url}")
    response = requests.get(subpage_url)
    sub_soup = BeautifulSoup(response.text,"html.parser")

    chair = sub_soup.find("h1") ## e.g. Entwicklungspsychologie
    chair_name = chair.get_text(strip=True)
    print(chair_name)

    tables = sub_soup.find_all("table", class_="basic") ## e.g. "Entwicklungspsychologie: Kinder- und Säuglingsalter"

    for i, table in enumerate(tables):
        print(f"\nTable {i+1} in {subpage_url}")
        table_data = []
        table_data.append(chair_name)
        rows = table.find_all("tr")

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
        
            cells = row.find_all(["th","td"])
            length = len(cells)
            print(f"\nlen: {length}")

            if length == 2:
                title = cells[0].get_text(strip=True) if len(cells) > 0 else ""
                table_data.append(title)
                link = cells[1].find("a",href=True)
                table_data.append(link)
                print(f"\niteration: {i}")
                print("Length = 2")
                print(f"\nTitle: {title}")
                print(f"\nLink: {link}")
                if link:
                    full_description = []
                    subsubpage_link = base_url + link["href"]
                    subresponse = requests.get(subsubpage_link)
                    subsub_soup = BeautifulSoup(subresponse.text, "html.parser")
                    description = subsub_soup.find("section", class_="ContentArea")
                    
                    if description:
                        section_text = description.get_text(strip=True, separator=" ")
                        full_description.append(section_text)
                        
                    else:
                        print("No section found")
                    description_text = " ".join(full_description)
                    table_data.append(description_text)
                    print(f"\ndescription: {description_text}")
            elif length == 1 and i == 1:
                print(f"\niteration: {i}")
                print("Length = 1")
                name = cells[0].get_text(strip=True) if len(cells) > 0 else ""
                print(f"\nName: {name}")
                table_data.append(name)
            elif length == 1 and i == 2:
                print(f"\niteration: {i}")
                print("Length = 1")
                position = cells[0].get_text(strip=True) if len(cells) > 0 else ""
                print(f"\nPosition: {position}")
                table_data.append(position)
            
            print(table_data)
            all_data.append(table_data)

df = pd.DataFrame(all_data)
df.to_csv("beautifulsoup.csv",index=False,sep=";",quoting=1,encoding="utf-8-sig")

title: IBT Colloquium
text:
Origin Ambiguity
Working Definition:

Origin Ambiguity: The blurring of provenance that occurs when AI-generated content resemble human-created content so closely that people struggle to tell who (or what) made them.



of note: ambiguity can also happen elsewhere, for example if you wonder if the content is fake


Origin Inference: A cognitive shift in which people prioritize identifying the source of a work (human or AI) over engaging with its meaning, quality, or message.


so what are we talking about?
people perceive some sort of origin ambiguity, which leads to engaging with the question who did this more than engaging with the question what was done

title: IBT Colloquium
text:
Origin Ambiguity




Survey of US adults in 2025 conducted by Pew Research Center (Fuentes 2025)




People want to know the origin, but few are able to identify it

participants are about as good as chance (Vukojičić, Krstić, and Veinović 2023) identifying AI-generated images
and slightly worse than chance (Porter and Machery 2024a) to slightly above chance with training at identifying text (Milička et al. 2025)




mention quote explicitly: *almost 50% of respondents can distinguish between AI and human** generated artwork.

“almost 50% of respondents can distinguish between AI and human generated artwork.” (Vukojičić, Krstić, and Veinović 2023)
“participants performed below chance levels in identifying AI-generated poems (46.6% accuracy)” (Porter and Machery 2024b)
“participants were more likely to judge AI-generated poems as human-authored than actual human-authored poems” (Porter and Machery 2024b)
With training, participants were able to correctly identify AI generated text correctly 65% of the time; without training 55% (Milička et al. 2025)

title: IBT Colloquium
text:
Theoretical Background
Preferences

humans \(>\) algorithms / “AI” (Bigman 2022; Kirk and Givi 2025; Lefkeli, Karataş, and Gürhan-Canli 2024, and others)
AI-generated content lowers purchase intentions and willingness to recommend a product (Kirk and Givi 2025; Belanche et al. 2025, and others)
AI-generated content decreases trust (Kirk and Givi 2025; Pfeuffer et al. 2025; Belanche et al. 2025)


But

negative effects are reduced if content is perceived as authentic regardless of origin (Silver, Newman, and Small 2021; Whittaker et al. 2025, and others)




It should also be acknowledged that Hartmann, Exner, and Domdey (2025) find that AI images are as good or better in terms of aestethics, realism, and quality, but this does not imply people LIKE them better
Humans generally prefer other humans over algorithms & AI (Bigman 2022; Kirk and Givi 2025; Lefkeli, Karataş, and Gürhan-Canli 2024, and others)
People are less willing to purchase products when communication is perceived to be written by AI (e.g., Kirk and Givi 2025), imagery is created by AI (e.g., Belanche et al. 2025)
Disclosure of use of AI decreases trust (Pfeuffer et al. 2025; Kirk and Givi 2025; Schilke and Reimann 2025)
humans alter their behavior in interaction with AI compared to other humans (Goergen, De Bellis, and Klesse 2025; Lefkeli, Karataş, and Gürhan-Canli 2024, and others)
preference for humans over AI is mitigated when AI-content is perceived as authentic (Silver, Newman, and Small 2021; Whittaker et al. 2025, and others)

title: IBT Colloquium
text:
Theoretical Background
Ambiguity Resolution in Marketing

ambiguity aversion \(\rightarrow\) preference for established products (Muthukrishnan, Wathieu, and Xu 2009)
ambiguous product quality
\(\rightarrow\) reliance on expectations instead of experience (Yi 1993)
\(\rightarrow\) more reliance on information from ads (Hoch and Ha 1986)
ambiguity in ads grabs attention (Kovacheva and Nikolova 2024; Peracchio and Meyers-Levy 1994; Johar 1995; Hagtvedt 2011; Sevilla and Meyer 2020) …
… especially when people are motivated to resolve this ambiguity for one reason or another (Johar 1995; Peracchio and Meyers-Levy 1994; Hagtvedt 2011)



ambiguity aversion also occurs in marketing: preference for established products under ambiguous conditions (Muthukrishnan, Wathieu, and Xu 2009)
ambiguous product quality leads to evaluation based on top-down expectations instead of bottom-up data-driven approach (Yi 1993)
ambiguous product quality leads to higher reliance on ads (Hoch and Ha 1986)
ambiguity as an attention grab works (Kovacheva and Nikolova 2024; Peracchio and Meyers-Levy 1994; Johar 1995; Hagtvedt 2011; Sevilla and Meyer 2020), but only when people are motivated to resolve this ambiguity for one reason or another (Johar 1995; Peracchio and Meyers-Levy 1994; Hagtvedt 2011)

title: IBT Colloquium
text:
Theoretical Background
Cognitive Tax of Ambiguity

ambiguity introduces cognitive taxes (Franceschetti et al. 2024; Shin, Kim, and Biocca 2019; Tao et al. 2022; Howard 2017)
\(\rightarrow\) cognitive taxes have a negative effect on evidence encoding and ability to retain information (e.g., Shou and Smithson 2015)
ambiguous stimuli (uncanny valley) introduce negative affect (Mori, MacDorman, and Kageki 2012; Seyama and Nagayama 2007, and others) and tax cognitive resources (Shin, Kim, and Biocca 2019; Tao et al. 2022; Howard 2017)



furthermore, there is evidence that different personality types have different needs to resolve ambiguous and obfuscated materials (Guigon, Villeval, and Dreher 2024; Kristofferson and Dunn 2023; Iannello et al. 2017)
we do know that it is not human

The uncanny valley hypothesis predicts a negative emotional appraisal of human replicas that appear or behave not quite human (Mori, MacDorman, and Kageki 2012)

ambiguous stimuli introduce negative affect (Mori, MacDorman, and Kageki 2012; Seyama and Nagayama 2007, and others) …
… and tax cognitive resources (Shin, Kim, and Biocca 2019; Tao et al. 2022; Howard 2017)

title: IBT Colloquium
text:
Intended Contribution

combination of streams of research: ambiguity in marketing (materials), cognitive load theory, and consumer-reaction to AI-generated content
relevance for both consumer-perspective and marketer-perspective:

does AI-generated content harm informed decision-making?
is AI-generated content effective?




combination of previously disjointed streams of research on ambiguity in marketing, on cognitive load theory, and on consumer exposure and reactions to AI-generated content.
Extending prior work on AI where origin is known or the variable in question, we study cases where humans face content that is neither declared AI or human or easily determined as one or the other
implications for both marketers and consumers: For marketers, potential backfiring of AI generated ads as well as the resulting trade-offs with efficiency and effectiveness are relevant. For consumers, cognitive resource reallocation might come at the cost of informed decision-making.

title: IBT Colloquium
text:
Research Plan
Detailed Information

ESF-SurveyCorrelational DataExperimental SetupNaturalistic Setup


\(\rightarrow\) Students in the ESF course are asked to scroll on TikTok and are asked how they perceive their media feed after.
Dimensions:

Origin ambiguity: To what extent do students question the origin of content?
Ambiguity Outcomes: To what extent does ambiguity influence enjoyment, trust, attention focus?
Differentiation: To what extent is “realness vs. fakeness” different from “human-made vs. AI generated”?



\(\rightarrow\) Demonstrate the occurrence and relevance of origin ambiguity in real life through existing correlational data
Possible Avenues:

What type of content is most susceptible to being questioned? Systematic searches on TikTok, Instagram (and co.) and subsequent classification
What type of user is most likely to question the origin?
Are these effect content- or platform-specific?



\(\rightarrow\) Demonstrate downstream effects of origin ambiguity through an experimental setup
Possible Downstream Effects:

Demonstrate reduced recall of content when participants are shown ambiguous marketing material
Demonstrate heightened attention (through eye-tracking, behavior tracking, …) when participants are exposed to ambiguous marketing material
…?

Possible Setups:

One-by-Two Designs: low vs. high origin
Naturalistic designs: DICE (Roggenkamp, Boegershausen, and Hildebrand 2025) to simulate more naturalistic environment
…?



\(\rightarrow\) Harness collaboration with real-life institution or industry partner to assess effects of origin ambiguity in real life
Possible Avenues:

Impressions, Clickthrough rates etc. of real-ads (A/B testing)
Recall of information for low vs. high origin ambiguity in target groups (e.g. through subscriptions, mailinglist, …)
…?
